utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. If I could remind you that the affirmation you made at the beginning of your evidence still applies. Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Bylykbashi, I want to continue where we left last evening, and that is you were testifying about being with Haradin Bala at the beginning of 1999 in Zabel. Do you recall that testimony?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER BYLYKBASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You may have to sit a little bit closer to the microphones so that the interpreters can hear you. And you testified that you were the leader of the group. That's correct, right?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER BYLYKBASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, in the beginning I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Until when?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER BYLYKBASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Approximately a month later I was appointed to go on another point.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What month would that have been?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER BYLYKBASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: End of February/beginning of March, to my recollection.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, is Agim Bylykbashi related to you?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER BYLYKBASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he's a relative of mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: How is he related to you?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER BYLYKBASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: We are blood related.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Was he also in Zabel in January, February of 1999?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER BYLYKBASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was there as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You testified that Haradin Bala's job was to observe the movements of the enemy. Correct?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER BYLYKBASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And he used binoculars?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER BYLYKBASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you recall Haradin Bala complaining about what other soldiers were doing or not doing at that time?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER BYLYKBASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't recall, not at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, I want to read to you some entries in his logbook from that time and see if it refreshes your recollection about some of his complaints about other soldiers. This is an entry from the 8th of February, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I would interpose --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] February.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I would be interposing at this point an objection with regards to relevance. We are now in the year of 1999, the month of February, some considerable months after the indictment period. I appreciate that cross-examination has wide latitude, however I believe we may be a bit far afield at this juncture.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think that the cross-examination that I'm going to pursue with respect to this time and the diary which is in evidence, it's P12, is relevant to the attitude of the accused Bala towards his job, towards other soldiers who were not doing his job, and I think this has all been made directly relevant by the evidence about -- the evidence and the arguments about the medical condition and the fact that he was unable to do work that the -- The cross-examination that I'm going to pursue and ask the witness about I think tends to show that the accused was very determined to do his job and to follow orders and to make sure that the work was done. And this -- one would not have expected this to be any different six months after the time period of the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Proceed for the moment, Mr. Whiting. If no clear relevance emerges, we may interrupt you again. So don't think you're quite out from the shadow of Mr. Guy-Smith's objection yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I appreciate that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: This is an entry from the 8th of February, 1999, and it's -- Mr. Bala writes: "I have a criticism regarding the doctors at Shale that have approved leave for one day for the following soldiers: Sheremet Kolshi, Xheme Bajraktari, Sef Bajraktari, Mehdi Krasniqi, Haki Ballagoshi. In my view, it is unnecessary for soldiers to take leave and return healthy and well from sick leave." Now, do you remember Mr. Bala at that time complaining about doctors giving sick leave to soldiers, and in particular the soldiers that I've just identified?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER BYLYKBASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember something related to this but it has been six years now that these events took place. Now, I can't tell you details, whether he complained to me or whether he wrote this only in his diary. I really can't help you with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, as the leader of the group, this would have been important, wouldn't it, if complaints about soldiers getting sick leave?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, I -- once again, now Mr. Whiting is suggesting that the witness speculate with regard to the internal writings of Mr. Bala. I don't believe in the first instance that the entry itself sheds any relevance with regard to any issues that are presented to the Court. Whether or not Mr. Bala felt that other people should or should not operate in a particular way or whether or not they should or should not have sick leave does not deal with the actuality of his particular physical condition and his motivations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The first part of that concern, Mr. Whiting, was conjecture.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Right. I wasn't asking the witness to speculate or engage in conjecture. I was asking him -- and I'll look at my question again, but what I intended to ask him is whether this would have been an important topic for him as the commander of the group, an important issue. And to some --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think it came across as being directed to whether it would have been important for Mr. Bala. You're saying now it's whether it was important for the witness. Is that what -- do I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That's what I intended to ask. "As leader of this group, this would have been important if complaints about soldiers getting sick leave." I intended to ask -- what I meant was be important to him as the leader of the group.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, this topic of soldiers getting sick leave and another soldier complaining about soldiers getting sick leave, that would have been an important topic to you as the commander of the group. Correct?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER BYLYKBASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is a misunderstanding regarding what you're saying. I don't know what Mr. Bala wrote in his diary. I didn't read his diary. I only heard that maybe there were complaints because, as I said, it has been six years now. But we didn't discuss the issue of sicks -- of sick leaves. So it only remained in that notebook where he wrote it and I don't remember him coming directly to me and complaining about these soldiers. It was a private matter for him and I don't know even myself why he wrote that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: But you did hear something about this at the time. Correct?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER BYLYKBASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what time where I heard it, whether at that moment or later, from a soldier who served with me together and then brought up this subject later on while we were serving somewhere else. So I really don't know in details.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. So what you're telling us is you can't remember when you heard this or what exactly you heard. Is that your testimony? Is that a fair summary of what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER BYLYKBASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Up to a point.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, what do you mean up to a point?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER BYLYKBASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I already told you, after you read this part, I remember that something was discussed in relation to what you read but I don't remember details.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And you also don't remember when it was discussed, whether it was at the time or later. Correct?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER BYLYKBASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember because in fact we did not discuss it. It's just that someone mentioned it. It's something that friends discussed amongst themselves. It's not that someone complained and then it became an issue that was discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Bala also writes in an entry for the 26th of February, 1999, that he had some difficulty with the person who was in charge of the 3rd Squad and he said: "The person in charge of the 3rd Squad threatened me using offensive words. Witnesses to this were Barllti, Fatmir, Muharrem, Luli being the fifth witness when Hamza attacked me physically also." Now, I take it you heard about this event?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Same objection, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Relevance do I take it is the point.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Just a minute, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, considering that the stated purpose for this line of examination. Especially in light of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Whiting, it's becoming less clear where this is leading us and how it's relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, the witness has testified in direct about specific memories. Now the witness has indicated some issues with respect to that, and I think I should be entitled to explore that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, you're now moving to credit. Is that it?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Continue, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, did you -- do you recall hearing about this event, the problem that Mr. Bala had with the person in charge of the 3rd Squad?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER BYLYKBASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What do you remember about it?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER BYLYKBASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just remember that there was a verbal argument with Mr. Hamza, whom he knew from before, and I think they were family related. But we didn't make an issue out of this problem and we just put an end to it without confusing or condemning any of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: How did you learn about it?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER BYLYKBASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but I can't remember how but I know this problem. It remained in my memory. I don't know that Mr. Bala informed me. I really don't know how I learned about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And did you solve the problem? Did you settle it as the commander or president leader of the group?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER BYLYKBASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: You should understand one thing. We were a bunch of friends that knew each other from long, long before, except for a few. But the others were all like friends and relatives, co-villagers. We solved all our problems by discussing them. We didn't come to a point when we couldn't understand each other any more. We just solved the problems on the spot.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I don't think you answered my question. My question was: Did you -- did you settle it -- or I'll rephrase it. Did you participate in the solving of the problem?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER BYLYKBASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see two questions here, whether I resolved it or whether I was part of the solution. Which do you want me to --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You're absolutely right, sir. Why don't we take them one at a time. Did you participate in solving the problem?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER BYLYKBASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you settle the problem?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER BYLYKBASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, together with the friends, with the comrades.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you remember when it happened?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER BYLYKBASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember. I don't remember the dates. It was during the period I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, finally it's written -- finally he writes: "Although soldier Haki Balagoshi was told not to take over the shift because that was to be done by the person in charge, the same ordered the soldier to do it without any reason only because he is lazy. The person in charge is Hamez Rexhepi." Now, do you -- sir, do you --

utterances.speaker: SKENDER BYLYKBASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me. Just a second.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I haven't asked the question yet.

utterances.speaker: SKENDER BYLYKBASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I didn't get the right translation or at least I didn't understand what you meant by "the shift." You meant maybe the change of the guard shift. This is what you meant?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I can only tell you what's written here, but that's perhaps what is meant and I'll read it again because the sentence is a little bit confusing. "Although soldier Haki Balagoshi was told not to take over the shift because that was to be done by the person in charge, the same ordered the soldier to do it without any reason only because he is lazy." And then it says: "The person in charge is Hamez Rexhepi, and the shift started at 2200 hours on 27th February, 1999." Now, do you recall Haradin Bala thinking that the person in charge was lazy?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER BYLYKBASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, this I don't remember. This sentence that you put to me, I don't remember. I don't recall to have heard it or to have read about it somewhere, because I think that was not very important for me to remember such things.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, let's go back to the Serb offensive that started on the 25th, 26th of July, 1998. You recall that offensive?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER BYLYKBASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, on the 26th.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You testified that you joined -- you testified here yesterday that you joined the KLA after that offensive. You remember that testimony?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER BYLYKBASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: During that offensive, on the -- not after the offensive but in the morning of the attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So the morning of the 26th or 25th?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER BYLYKBASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably you have notes. I know that the date when the air-strikes started -- sorry, apologies, when the shelling started, I know that I went to the positions. The date, you must know it better.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Where did you join?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER BYLYKBASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I joined it with some friends who came -- who had come from Albania one day earlier. We went to Laz -- Fanat Te Llazet, a place which is 3 or 4 kilometres away from the village as the crow flies.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: 3 to 4 kilometres away from Bajince?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER BYLYKBASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe 2 or 3, not 4. But the place is well-known.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. 2 or 3, though, from Bajince?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER BYLYKBASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is possible that it is 2 or 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: In which direction?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER BYLYKBASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: East, in the direction of Magure, in the east.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Where did you get the gun?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER BYLYKBASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: A friend of mine brought me the gun. He is also a neighbour of mine. He brought it from Albania. It was a rifle, a 20-millimetre rifle.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You also testified here that after the Serb offensive you and Haradin Bala were at the same point in Bajince.

utterances.speaker: SKENDER BYLYKBASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, two or three days later. Not two or three days later, but when we returned from Zborce.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, in fact it was some weeks later, wasn't it, it was a number of weeks after the beginning of the offensive that Haradin Bala came back to Bajince, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER BYLYKBASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have misunderstood it because I don't think I said it. On the day that we went to Zborce in the morning on the day of the shelling, we were waiting to go to Lapusnik, but we went to Zborce together with a group of friends to protect the place from a possible attack from that area. Because the place where we were was surrounded by a range of mountains and fearing that the Serbs might attack us from that point, we went there. We stayed there until the evening. In the evening at about 12.00, a soldier came and told us that the Lapusnik gorge had fallen and that he -- he told us that it's better for you to go back to your own gorge. And this is what we did, we went back to the gorge where the population had taken shelter. In the beginning, it was a chaotic situation because everybody was taken by surprise that the Lapusnik gorge would one day fall, which they had learned then. But soon we started to organise ourselves, and either on the next day or the day after that, the population returned to the village, whereas we remained there -- in the mountains. We divided in two groups to protect the population. We -- there were two groups, but we kept in contact. We switched places. Sometimes we went closer to the village; sometimes we went to the mountains. This is how we stayed. We stayed there for two or three weeks, and then we went back to the village and then stayed in a room, in oda. Those whose houses were near went sometimes to sleep at their own homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I understand. What I'm putting to you is that after you returned to Bajince from Zborce, Haradin Bala did not come to Bajince and stay in Bajince until -- for some weeks, until the end of August. Correct?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER BYLYKBASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are saying this. No, that's not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So what is your testimony about when he came?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER BYLYKBASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: My testimony is that I have seen him. I didn't see only Haradin Bala, but also other friends like Agim, Ramadan Krasniqi, who used to be in Pjetershtice. They, too, came to the gorge. In fact, it was -- it was kind of disintegration of the army and everybody went to protect either the family or the village they were living, where they knew the terrain better. And since Haradin Bala's family was in Bajince, he did the same. Whether he came that day, I am not sure. It was night because almost everybody went to join their own families to see how they were doing. On the next day, we divided in two groups and went not to points because there were no points there, but in secret places in the mountains.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What I'm trying to focus on is when, according to your memory, when he came to Bajince, in relation to the offensive on Lapusnik and the fall of Lapusnik gorge. Was it a day or two? Was it longer than that? What is your memory?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER BYLYKBASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but I think I found Haradin Bala there on the day when I returned from Zborce. Two days ago or three days ago before going to meet my comrades in Malisheve, I saw him in passing in the yard of his own relative. I don't know exactly whether he stayed there because it was a confused situation. Some of us went to look for weapons, and I don't know whether he stayed in the village or -- but the most important thing is that after the fall of the Lapusnik gorge, we did what we did. And then afterwards we returned to the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. So just to be clear, you returned from Zborce within a day or two after the fall of Lapusnik and you saw Haradin Bala there in Bajince. That's your testimony?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER BYLYKBASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I returned from Zborce on the day that Lapusnik fell. It was after midnight probably and we found an empty village. We went to the gorge and it was there that we saw the population. This is the truth. And I have seen Haradin Bala either the next day or the day after that because, you know, six years have passed since then when we all got together as soldiers and were trying to figure out what we were going to do under those circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And is it your testimony that after you saw Haradin Bala either the next day or the day of that he stayed in Bajince with you through August, through September, through the fall until the end of the year? Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER BYLYKBASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's the truth. Maybe he may have gone away for a weekend or when he may have been sick, but most of the time we've been together. We've acted together.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, in fact, don't you recall that towards the end of the year Mr. Bala was in Luznica? Towards the end of the year 1998 into the new year, Mr. Bala was in Luznica? Don't you recall that? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: SKENDER BYLYKBASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, I don't recall that. It can't be. If you are talking about the year until the end of the year, this cannot be.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Since you know Haradin Bala, can you give us any possible reason why he would have said at the end of the year that he was in Luznica and had been given leave to see his family in Bajince? That he was serving in Luznica and had been given leave to go to see his family in Bajince? Can you give us -- are you -- do you know any reason why he might have said that at the end of the year, 1998?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER BYLYKBASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. It may be a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: A mistake by whom?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER BYLYKBASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know whose mistake, but he cannot be in two places at the same time. He was in Bajince. He acted there after the offensive. We were together for a long time. Sometimes I was away, but it was something I did within the same day. And in the evening, I returned back. So I remember the place we stayed together, the room with him and with other comrades.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If I might rise, I assume there is a basis for the question as being asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Day 30, page 3086.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Bala said this.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Let's go back to June and July of 1998. And first of all, before I ask you questions about that time period, there is a road that runs from Bajince to Nekovce, up to Kishna Reka. Correct?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER BYLYKBASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Once you reach Kishna Reka, you can either continue driving to Lapusnik or you can even walk to Lapusnik. Correct?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER BYLYKBASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It depends. I don't know from Kizhareke to Lapusnik to walk, I think walking is the only way. It takes you about two hours because it's a very steep road.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With all due respect, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: -- if I might ask my esteemed colleague to double-check his reference site because I see that the transcript goes up to page 84 on Day 30.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm sorry it's Day 34 --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Page?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If the witness could be shown image 8 of P1, please. We have -- yeah, no that's fine. And if it could be placed on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, if you could look at that map, if it could be placed on the ELMO, please. It's probably easier if you look at it on your -- to your left, not on the computer. Don't -- if -- it's easier if you go ahead and look at it. Now, this is an aerial photograph of Lapusnik. Do you recognise it?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER BYLYKBASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: More or less.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The -- in the lower right of the -- of the image, do you see a few houses there?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER BYLYKBASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The lower right.

utterances.speaker: SKENDER BYLYKBASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here, this corner here?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Right, those houses. Those houses belong to Kishna Reka. Right?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER BYLYKBASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, this road that's right there that we see going from the top of the image between 489000 and 489500 down to the lower right of the image, that road is the road that goes to Kishna Reka, Nekovce, Bajince. Correct?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER BYLYKBASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The road up here?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: No, no, no. That's the Peja-Pristina road. The road that comes -- that road. That road is the road that goes to Kishna Reka, Nekovce, Bajince. Correct?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER BYLYKBASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This here?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: SKENDER BYLYKBASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. That's the road that goes to Kishna Reka-Bajince. Correct?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER BYLYKBASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think so. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Your previous answer wasn't picked up by the interpreters. Now -- and that is in fact Kishna Reka in the lower right of the image there, those houses that you pointed at. Those houses are Kishna Reka. Correct?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER BYLYKBASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is part of Kishna Reka and it could also be part of Komorane.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, it would not take two hours, would it, to walk from those houses to Lapusnik, would it?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER BYLYKBASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It depends how you travel because now by car you can go very fast. There are newly built roads. But at that time you had to go through the gorge, through the other side of the gorge and get up here.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: No, I'm talking about walking. You could walk from those houses in the lower right of the image to Lapusnik in a short time. Correct?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER BYLYKBASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. First of all, this part here, these houses you referred to, I'm not sure whether it is Kishna Reka indeed because they can be houses of Komorane, of old Komorane as they call it. Kishna Reka should be more in the inner part. I have gone to Berisa through this part on foot and it took me about two hours because of the steep road. I'm speaking of my experience.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm not sure if you focussed on my question. My question is: Whatever village those houses belong to in the lower right of the image, it would not take two hours to walk from those houses into Lapusnik. Right?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER BYLYKBASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your testimony is it would take two hours to walk from those houses to the village of Lapusnik?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER BYLYKBASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm telling you that it depends who is walking. As I'm a fit person, it takes me about one hour and a half to get there. It's not easy to walk up there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You can -- that can be taken away. I'm done with that map.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, turning to June and July, you testified that you were not in the KLA at that time because you did not have a gun.

utterances.speaker: SKENDER BYLYKBASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. Until the 26th of July I wasn't a soldier of the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And that was because you did not have a gun. Correct?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER BYLYKBASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was the reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: There were KLA soldiers in your village, correct, in June and July of 1998?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER BYLYKBASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there weren't.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: There were no KLA soldiers in Bajince in June and July of 1998?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER BYLYKBASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there weren't. There were soldiers from Bajince serving at another point.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Were there KLA soldiers in Kishna Reka in June and July of 1998?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER BYLYKBASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Were there KLA soldiers in Nekovce in June and July of 1998?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER BYLYKBASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew one person who was from Nekovce. I don't know where he was stationed, at what point, but I knew a person from Nekovce who was a soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: There were KLA soldiers in Shale, Sedlare, correct, in June and July of 1998?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER BYLYKBASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm really sorry, but I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: During this time, June and July of 1998, that was a time when people were joining the KLA, correct? If they had a weapon or if they could get a weapon, they were joining during that time, June and July of 1998. Right?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER BYLYKBASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, those who felt themselves as Albanians, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, you were asked by Mr. Guy-Smith about how many times you saw Haradin Bala in your village during June and July of 1998, and your response was this, this was yesterday: "I may have seen him four or five times. I cannot be sure because I know I have seen him later as well." So it's hard to be sure when exactly things happened. Correct?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER BYLYKBASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I already told you, it could be four or five times. It could be four times and one time later on. I don't know the exact number, but as I said it was four or five times that I saw him, that I noticed him.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And in fact, the conversation, the brief conversation that you recounted -- that you say you remember with Haradin Bala about Luznica, that could have happened later, couldn't it?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER BYLYKBASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No because it is connected with the flour, with the food that he brought about -- for his family. After the 26th of July, I was no longer interested who was bringing flour because I became a soldier. Someone else took up the responsibility for the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You were still in the village, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER BYLYKBASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which period are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: After the 26th of July. You were still in Bajince, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER BYLYKBASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said earlier, we were for two or three weeks around Bajince. We didn't contact with co-villagers except for some young men who brought us food.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So food was -- continued to be an issue, of course, after the 26th of July?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER BYLYKBASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, you never saw Haradin Bala in Luznica in June and July 1998. Correct?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER BYLYKBASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but I was never at Luznica.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You were never in Luznica in June and July of 1998. Correct? You --

utterances.speaker: SKENDER BYLYKBASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not even now. Until recently, I've never been to Luznica.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you know that to travel to Luznica you had -- from Bajince, you had to drive down to Shale, Sedlare, then to Klecka and then to Luznica? Did you know that at the time?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER BYLYKBASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure whether the road was open at that time and whether you could go by car. I'm really not sure because I never went there through Shale.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: When Haradin Bala came to Bajince during June and July of 1998, how did he come, if you know?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER BYLYKBASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw him once when he came with a car - I think it was a Lada - that time when I asked him about the flour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: When is the first time you told the story about remembering this conversation with Haradin Bala?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I think I will interpose an objection to the characterisation of the witness's testimony. I don't know whether or not Mr. Whiting was being, shall we say, dramatic, in the use of the term "story" or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I didn't mean to be dramatic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: When is -- when is the first time you recounted this conversation about Luznica with Haradin Bala? When is the first time you told somebody about that?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER BYLYKBASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand the last part. If you could repeat it, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I certainly can, and I'll try to make it more clear. You -- when is the first time you told somebody about this conversation you say you had with Haradin Bala about Luznica?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER BYLYKBASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if I discussed it with anybody except with the Defence team when I gave them my statement. I don't remember discussing it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And when did you give your statement?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER BYLYKBASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Approximately four months ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: In February of 2003, you knew that Haradin Bala had been arrested by the Tribunal. Correct?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER BYLYKBASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I heard about it, if he was arrested in February 2003.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And I take it you have followed the case in the newspapers or on television in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: SKENDER BYLYKBASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You haven't at all followed this case?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER BYLYKBASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not at all I haven't followed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You weren't interested in what Haradin Bala was being charged with and what was happening to him?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER BYLYKBASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's a difference here. Personally I didn't have the possibility to follow the trial because it is sometimes shown on television in the evening. I work till 6.00, 7.00, then spend with my children two or three hours and then go to sleep in order to be able to wake up at 6.00 in the morning for work.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: But you knew when Haradin Bala was arrested that he was being arrested for -- and he was accused of committing crimes in Lapusnik in the summer of 2000 -- of 1998. Correct? You certainly knew that, right?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER BYLYKBASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I heard about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And you heard about that when he was arrested, correct, sometime in 2003?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER BYLYKBASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm really sorry. I did hear that he was arrested, but I really don't know whether I heard on the very day of the arrest or whether I heard later from a friend of mine. But what I know is I heard about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Whether it was on the day of the arrest or a day or two later, it was around the time that he got arrested that you heard about it. Correct?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER BYLYKBASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure. Please don't take me to where I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you think you heard about it in 2003, what he was arrested for, that he was arrested for committing crimes in Lapusnik? Do you think you heard about that sometime in 2003?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER BYLYKBASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: But you're not even sure about that. Correct?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER BYLYKBASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a minute. I'm really sorry. I am sure that I heard about his arrest, but as I said earlier I don't remember dates and periods of time except for those that are really important for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, you've just told us that four months ago you made a statement to the Defence lawyers, and in that statement you told them about what happened to you and to Haradin Bala in 1998. Correct?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER BYLYKBASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. What happened in 1998, that's what I told them. And there I based myself on a very important day for myself, and that was when I got my weapon.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And you were careful to be accurate and truthful with them, correct, when you talked to them four months ago?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER BYLYKBASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not that I'm being careful whether to be accurate or not; this is the truth. These are things that I have experienced and there's no way I could be wrong about them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, in fact, didn't you tell the Defence lawyers four months ago that you joined the KLA at the beginning of May 1998?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER BYLYKBASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never. I assisted the KLA, but I wasn't a KLA soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, there's a clear difference, and you've made that clear difference here in court, between assisting the KLA and joining the KLA. Right?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER BYLYKBASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never said I was a soldier, member of the KLA, before the 26th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. See, because we get -- the Defence lawyers give us a summary of what you're going to testify to. We don't get your statement, but we get a summary. And according to your summary it says: "The witness will testify he joined the KLA at the time the Serb forces launched their attack on Lapusnik in the beginning of May 1998." Did you tell the Defence lawyers that?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER BYLYKBASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is wrong. This is either your mistake or their mistake. I have never said I joined the KLA in May because the offensive on Lapusnik started on the 26th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, didn't you also tell the Defence lawyers that in fact Haradin Bala moved his family to Bajince before the 9th of May, 1998?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER BYLYKBASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember this at all. I don't recollect this date at all. I never knew the exact date when his family arrived. And as I told you, I relate everything to that crucial date that I mentioned in my life.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, in this summary it says -- and I'll just read it to you: "Because of the danger of Serb attacks, the accused Haradin Bala moved his family to Bajince for shelter. The witness will testify that this happened prior to the Serb offensive on Lapusnik." And I checked to make sure that was referring to the 9th of May, 1998. So are you sure that you didn't tell the Defence lawyers that Haradin Bala moved his family to Bajince before the 9th of May, 1998?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER BYLYKBASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: If someone insisted on the 9th of May, you may say so. I don't know how they have linked it, but I simply said that he moved his family because the family was in danger in Korretice where it was living, and that place was close to the road, very exposed to danger, and that the Serbs might have intervened quickly there. So for the family to escape the danger, he moved it to Bajince. I didn't say the 9th of May. If they insisted on the date, I don't know how they came up with the date, but I didn't say that date.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, what is your testimony about what happened? What is your testimony now about what happened, about when he moved the family to Bajince?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER BYLYKBASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: He moved his family to Bajince before the 26th of July. Whether it was three weeks, two weeks, or two months ago, I don't know for sure. But I know it was there for that date.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And you first met Haradin Bala as the husband of Mrs. Bala, who was from the village of Bajince. Correct?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER BYLYKBASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct. I didn't know him before. I knew him only by sight and I knew that he was married to a lady from that village, but I didn't have any closer contact with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And you don't remember when he moved his family to Bajince? That's your testimony now, that you don't remember when he moved his family to Bajince?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER BYLYKBASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that his family moved there before the 26th of July, but as to when exactly it was I cannot tell you for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Whiting. Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I want to matter sure that matters are clear, and if I have made a mistake in any regard I apologise and I want to make sure that we understand what you remember, what you experienced, and what did you did not, based upon what -- the questions you've been asked both by myself as well as by Mr. Whiting. Okay. On July 26th, 1998, do you recall whether or not there was an offensive in which the -- what has been called the Lapusnik gorge fell?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER BYLYKBASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember it very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Before the Lapusnik gorge fell, where were you?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER BYLYKBASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in Bajince village.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: While you were in Bajince village, did you have occasion to see Haradin Bala's family or not?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER BYLYKBASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yeah, I saw them in passing, outside in the yard.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: When you were at your village before the fall of the Lapusnik gorge on July 26th, did you have a conversation with Haradin Bala or not in which the topic of food arose?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER BYLYKBASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I did. It was then that we talked about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Apart from having a conversation with Mr. Bala concerning the topic of food, did you have occasion to see Haradin Bala in your village of Bajince before the fall of Lapusnik gorge?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER BYLYKBASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I saw him two or three times, apart from that conversation I had. And we have met many more times later.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: When did you become a member of the KLA as a soldier?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER BYLYKBASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 26th of July, 1998, in the morning of that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Why didn't you become a member of the KLA as a soldier before July 26th in the morning?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER BYLYKBASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because there weren't enough weapons in the territory where we lived. It was hard for us to get a weapon. We had to go to Albania to be able to fetch one, and it was very difficult trip to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Have you had the opportunity to have a weapon before the 26th of July, would you have joined the KLA before that time?

utterances.speaker: SKENDER BYLYKBASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: But I do have one comment to make with regard to Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the matter on page 3086 in which a statement is attributed to my client which is a hearsay statement made by someone else. I have some concerns about the manner in which the question was posed because it assumes that in fact the statement was made. I understand the extent to which hearsay is allowed in these proceedings, but I ask the Court in its consideration of this particular question and answer, to the extent it's going to impact at all with regard to this witness's testimony, to take heed and care.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir. That is the end of the questions that are asked of you by counsel. We thank you for your attendance. You are now free to return to your home and work.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Goodbye.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We note your observation, Mr. Guy-Smith, and I take it this is probably a convenient time or would you think it useful to spend quarter of an hour with the next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I think this is a convenient time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well. We will have the first break now, resuming at 10 minutes to 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, prior to us calling our next witness, who Mr. Harvey will be questioning, I have a brief comment to make and I've been requested specifically by Mr. Bala to make this comment, which is that he would greatly appreciate when any statements are attributed to him that if they're not statements that he made directly that the author of the statement or where the statement came from be identified, because it caused him some concern and he did not feel it appropriate in his mind. I have raised the matter with Mr. Whiting, I have told him I would be raising the matter with the Court before we started. I think Mr. Whiting understands our position and I believe that I understand his position with regard to the manner in which he chooses to ask questions. But since the issue was raised by Mr. Bala and he specifically asked he to raise it with the Court, I am doing so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You anticipated what would have been the Chamber's reaction in what you've gone on to say. And could I observe that with respect to the comment you made before we broke, the matter that was the subject of the question was in evidence. It therefore forms properly the basis for questioning. What, if any, weight might be attached to it is a very different question and that we will have to consider at the end of evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I appreciate both that as well as the Court's comments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The next witness is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Mr. Kadri Dugoli.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Dugoli. Would you please read aloud the affirmation that the on the card that is given to you now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, sir. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Please sit down. Mr. Harvey has some questions for you. Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Dugoli.

utterances.speaker: KADRI DUGOLI
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: I take it from your reply that you're hearing my questions clearly and you are able to follow the translation.

utterances.speaker: KADRI DUGOLI
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Where do you live, in which village?

utterances.speaker: KADRI DUGOLI
utterances.text: I live in Nekovce, in Drenoc municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: And have you lived there all of your life?

utterances.speaker: KADRI DUGOLI
utterances.text: Yes, with the exception of a time, that is two years, I was staying with my uncles in Korretice e Eperme at Haradin's father's.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: And who is or was your uncle?

utterances.speaker: KADRI DUGOLI
utterances.text: His name is Selman Bala. He is the father of Haradin Bala. My mother and he were brother and sister.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: So that makes you and Haradin first cousins, if I'm right?

utterances.speaker: KADRI DUGOLI
utterances.text: I don't know what you're saying about first cousins, but I know that he is the son of my uncle. Yes, I think you're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Okay. And I hope you won't find this offensive, but I think you're older than he is?

utterances.speaker: KADRI DUGOLI
utterances.text: No -- you think older than Haradin?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: KADRI DUGOLI
utterances.text: Yes, I am some seven years older than him I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: And as children, did you grow up together, given that age difference?

utterances.speaker: KADRI DUGOLI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: And did your families visit each other on a frequent basis?

utterances.speaker: KADRI DUGOLI
utterances.text: Yes. On a very frequent basis. Sometimes I went to visit his family, sometimes he came to visit my family.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: And there came a time in your life, did there, when you had to do military service?

utterances.speaker: KADRI DUGOLI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Do you remember which years those were?

utterances.speaker: KADRI DUGOLI
utterances.text: 1969, 1970, and then I was released in 1971. The military service lasted 18 months.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: And after that, do you know where Haradin was working, or if he was working.

utterances.speaker: KADRI DUGOLI
utterances.text: Haradin was working before he got sick. He was working in a construction enterprise in Drenoc, but I don't know the year when he started work there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Do you remember him falling ill?

utterances.speaker: KADRI DUGOLI
utterances.text: Yes, very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: What happened there that you remember?

utterances.speaker: KADRI DUGOLI
utterances.text: I remember that Haradin was ill. He was complaining of the left side of his eyes and hand and then -- arm. And then after a week they took him to neuropsychiatric hospital I think and they thought he had some sort of paralysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Who took him there?

utterances.speaker: KADRI DUGOLI
utterances.text: I don't know who took him there, but I know that I went to visit him after five or six days and that he couldn't move. I stayed for half an hour with him and then I went home.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: So you visited him in hospital. I know it's hard to remember the dates exactly --

utterances.speaker: KADRI DUGOLI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Do you remember roughly which year that would have been in?

utterances.speaker: KADRI DUGOLI
utterances.text: It was before the 1990s. To tell you the truth, I cannot recollect when it was because a long time has passed since then.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Was there only one occasion when you visited him in hospital or more than one?

utterances.speaker: KADRI DUGOLI
utterances.text: I was there two times.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: And was the second time during that same year or was it at a different period altogether?

utterances.speaker: KADRI DUGOLI
utterances.text: During the first time I visited him in hospital. After that, I visited him on two other occasions. I don't know what year it was. He was again in hospital in Pristina. I think he was in the intensive care unit, and there they told him that he had a heart infarction or attack, as you might say, but that he was in a dangerous state. He couldn't leave the room for five or six days and we were not allowed to visit him there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: So you've told us that the first time he was taken to hospital was you believed before the 1990s. Was this second occasion also before the 1990s or sometime in the 1990s?

utterances.speaker: KADRI DUGOLI
utterances.text: I don't remember very well, but I think it was -- the first time was the 1990s. The second time was not after a long time, but it was probably in the same year. I know that he was very sick and he was hospitalised.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: So we have two periods of hospitalisation. Are you aware whether he was ever hospitalised on any other occasion after that?

utterances.speaker: KADRI DUGOLI
utterances.text: I think he went to Albania. He was hospitalised in Albania before the war, and I know that he was again hospitalised after the war and again for his heart condition.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Just dealing with the one before the war, taking the war as being -- as beginning in 1998, do you have any sense today of how long before the war, months or years?

utterances.speaker: KADRI DUGOLI
utterances.text: If I'm not mistaken, it may have been in 1992/1993. The others, I don't remember. I know that they were before the 1990s.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. I'd -- I'd like to try and get my voice working properly first. Now, let's try that one again. I'd now like to move forward to the war. Did you know Haradin's family?

utterances.speaker: KADRI DUGOLI
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: And did you know where his wife came from, which village her family came from?

utterances.speaker: KADRI DUGOLI
utterances.text: His wife came from Bajince village, Lipjan municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Now, once the war started, did his family stay in Korretice e Eperme?

utterances.speaker: KADRI DUGOLI
utterances.text: It was sometime -- I think it was on the 8th of May when Haradin brought his family to stay with my own family. So they stayed in my home. He stayed there -- they stayed there for some two weeks.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: KADRI DUGOLI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: And when you say his family, about how many family members did he bring?

utterances.speaker: KADRI DUGOLI
utterances.text: They are a large family, but his narrow family with his two brothers were staying at my house, whereas some other brothers and their mothers stayed with my brother.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: And when you say they stayed with your brother, was that also in the village of Nekovce?

utterances.speaker: KADRI DUGOLI
utterances.text: We live very close with my brother. We share the same wall, maybe 50, 60 metres away.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... close family to you, did he -- did he stay with you or did he go off himself?

utterances.speaker: KADRI DUGOLI
utterances.text: That night he stayed there. He was tired. On the next day, he set off.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: And how long after that roughly, if you remember, how long was it before you saw him again?

utterances.speaker: KADRI DUGOLI
utterances.text: Maybe after four or five days. Haradin, five or six, he came back to me and he brought food supplies for his family.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: And did he then go away again?

utterances.speaker: KADRI DUGOLI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: And when was -- about how long after that did you see him again?

utterances.speaker: KADRI DUGOLI
utterances.text: He came back another time -- or two times after he left the family there, and then after two weeks he came and took his family to Bajince with his brother and some food supplies that were still there. He took them -- he took them to Bajince.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: And after he'd taken his family to Bajince, how long after that was it before you saw him again?

utterances.speaker: KADRI DUGOLI
utterances.text: I saw him at the end of May in Bajince village. I went there and stayed for less than an hour. We talked together. We lit a cigarette. He complained to me about his health. He was ill. He always took his medicine, I don't know what kind of medicine.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: He was ill but he was still smoking?

utterances.speaker: KADRI DUGOLI
utterances.text: He has never quit smoking. I don't know about now, whether he still smokes, even though the doctor has recommended him to quit smoking. I think he takes after his father, who never quitted smoking and was hospitalised a couple of times.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: I know. We've tried to stop him, too; it doesn't work, does it? So that time when you saw him at the end of May in Bajince, did you see him with his family or separate from his family?

utterances.speaker: KADRI DUGOLI
utterances.text: He was with his family, but I went there, stayed for a while with his family. And when I left he was staying in the shade because he could never stand in the sun. He was staying in the shade. We stayed together for some time, then I went home. I don't know what he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: You say he couldn't stay in the -- he couldn't stand the sun.

utterances.speaker: KADRI DUGOLI
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Did you ever observe him -- well, let me put that another way. Has he -- how did he tolerate the heat in the summer?

utterances.speaker: KADRI DUGOLI
utterances.text: Since he was ill for the first time, he always took an umbrella with him to keep it when he was hot and it was sun.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: So you would see him walking along in the sun with an umbrella up over his head?

utterances.speaker: KADRI DUGOLI
utterances.text: He used -- he didn't walk a lot, and when he did he always took with him an umbrella, but usually he drove.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Do you happen to remember what sort of car you saw him driving?

utterances.speaker: KADRI DUGOLI
utterances.text: When do you think?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Thank you for putting it that way. When did you see him driving a car?

utterances.speaker: KADRI DUGOLI
utterances.text: After the war -- I meant not a real car. I meant a cart. It is horse-drawn.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: When did you see him with a buggy or a horse-drawn cart? When was that?

utterances.speaker: KADRI DUGOLI
utterances.text: All the time -- every time I saw him, he was travelling in his buggy because he couldn't walk. He was very ill.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Does that go for before the war as well as after the war?

utterances.speaker: KADRI DUGOLI
utterances.text: Before the war, after the war he had a car; his brother bought it for him. So the time he took me with him when I wanted to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... horse-drawn buggy; after the war, his brother bought him a car?

utterances.speaker: KADRI DUGOLI
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Finally this: Did you ever join the KLA?

utterances.speaker: KADRI DUGOLI
utterances.text: No, I couldn't join the KLA, but I rendered as much assistance as I could to it. I didn't have a uniform and I never joined it. This is why I am saying I didn't join, because in one way or another all the Albanians assisted the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Fine. If you would remain there, please, there will be some more questions for you. Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Mansfield.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: No question, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Topolski.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Black.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Hi, Mr. Dugoli, I'm standing to your right. My name is Mr. Black. Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: KADRI DUGOLI
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I gather from what you've testified to here today that you're a cousin with Haradin Bala. That's correct?

utterances.speaker: KADRI DUGOLI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And in addition to that would you say that you're also friends with him?

utterances.speaker: KADRI DUGOLI
utterances.text: Very close friends indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Did Haradin Bala ever talk to you about his determination to join the KLA in 1998?

utterances.speaker: KADRI DUGOLI
utterances.text: No, we didn't talk about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: So you --

utterances.speaker: KADRI DUGOLI
utterances.text: We were all determined to join the KLA but we couldn't, all of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Well, you mentioned that, that you yourself weren't able to join the KLA; why was that?

utterances.speaker: KADRI DUGOLI
utterances.text: I wasn't able to join the KLA because there weren't sufficient weapons. I couldn't go and get one or buy one, and that's why I didn't join.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And you said you rendered assistance in other ways. Can you give me any examples of how you assisted the KLA?

utterances.speaker: KADRI DUGOLI
utterances.text: Yes. In the beginning, we stood guard duty together with the soldiers, and we helped them in observing. We also helped them with food. We would bring them food and water to the mountains.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. And do you remember when you first learned that Haradin Bala had joined the KLA?

utterances.speaker: KADRI DUGOLI
utterances.text: Only when he brought his family at my place. He told me that he was going to Lapusnik. It was in the beginning of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Do you remember the words that he used? Did he describe his motivation in any way?

utterances.speaker: KADRI DUGOLI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you talked earlier about a couple incidents in May 1998 when you saw Haradin Bala. Do you remember that? Do you remember testifying about that?

utterances.speaker: KADRI DUGOLI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And just to make sure that I have the chronology correct, you said the first time I believe was on the 8th of May, 1998. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: KADRI DUGOLI
utterances.text: I said it was between the 6th and the 8th of May, 7th, 8th, 6th, I don't remember the exact date. This is what I said earlier. So it was between the 6th and the 8th of May. I don't remember which day it was exactly. We celebrate a holiday back home which is between the 6th and the 8th of May. And that's why I remember this date because on the 9th of May, many refugees came to our village and when Haradin saw that many people were staying in my house, he then decided to take his family to his in-laws.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Well, let me just go one step at a time to make sure I'm clear about all this. Do you remember perhaps which day of the week it was? I know you don't know whether it was the 6th the 7th, or the 8th, but do you happen to remember what day of the week it was?

utterances.speaker: KADRI DUGOLI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. So that holiday that you celebrate during that time, it doesn't always -- and I'm just asking, I don't know, it doesn't always fall on a Saturday or always fall on a Tuesday or anything like that?

utterances.speaker: KADRI DUGOLI
utterances.text: It falls on an exact date, regardless of the day. It's on the 6th, and it's celebrated on the 6th, 7th, and 8th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I understand. And your testimony is that you first saw Haradin Bala in May 1998 sometime during that holiday, during those three days, is that right, but you don't remember which day in particular?

utterances.speaker: KADRI DUGOLI
utterances.text: I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Let me try to be more clear about it. Your testimony is that during that holiday that's celebrated on the 6th, 7th, and 8th, at some point on those three days you saw Haradin Bala. Am I correct about that?

utterances.speaker: KADRI DUGOLI
utterances.text: I didn't meet with him. What I said was that he brought his family from Korretice village to my village, village of Nekovce, his immediate family and his extended family. In my place, Haradin's family was staying and the families of his two brothers.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. I understand. And you -- but you personally saw him. You met with him in that sense that you saw him and actually talked to him. Right?

utterances.speaker: KADRI DUGOLI
utterances.text: Yes, we talked.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Do you remember when Haradin Bala and his family arrived, do you remember how they arrived? Did they arrive in -- all together in one vehicle or in several vehicles? What kind of vehicles? Do you remember anything about that?

utterances.speaker: KADRI DUGOLI
utterances.text: Some came in a tractor, some on horse-drawn carts, some on foot.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: You don't remember any cars at that time?

utterances.speaker: KADRI DUGOLI
utterances.text: We didn't have any other vehicle except for tractors.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: When you say "we didn't have any other vehicle except for tractors," who do you mean by "we"? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: KADRI DUGOLI
utterances.text: I mean Haradin and myself, his family and my family.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: What about -- when you say "Haradin's family," what about his brothers? Did any of his brothers have cars before the war or during the war?

utterances.speaker: KADRI DUGOLI
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't remember. A brother of his who was in Italy, he had but he would buy cars and sell cars.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Did you ever see Haradin Bala in any of those cars?

utterances.speaker: KADRI DUGOLI
utterances.text: You mean in his brother's cars?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: KADRI DUGOLI
utterances.text: I don't know. Sometimes, yes, we drove together with his brother, who was working abroad in Italy.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. And just to be clear on the time, that was before or during the war. Correct?

utterances.speaker: KADRI DUGOLI
utterances.text: Before the war. During the war, his brother was in Italy and his car was not there. I refer to Haradin's oldest brother; he had the car.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Do you remember what kind of car he had?

utterances.speaker: KADRI DUGOLI
utterances.text: He once had an Alpha Romeo and then a Kadett. I don't really know all the makes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And you testified that Haradin Bala -- on this first occasion he stayed the night and then he left the next day. Right?

utterances.speaker: KADRI DUGOLI
utterances.text: Yes, in the morning. He left my house in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Do you remember how he left, by what mode of transportation?

utterances.speaker: KADRI DUGOLI
utterances.text: I don't remember whether he went on a tractor or other type of vehicle, but I know that he didn't go on foot.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. And then the next time that you saw him I think you said was four to six days later. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: KADRI DUGOLI
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I think you told us how long he stayed -- well, maybe you didn't. How long did he stay at your house on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: KADRI DUGOLI
utterances.text: If we are talking about the second time, he spent the night in my house. He brought food supplies for his family, and he brought a box of cigarettes for his wife because she smokes, too. He taught her how to smoke. It was a box of Holiday cigarettes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Do you remember anything about the food supplies that he bought -- brought, excuse me? What did he bring?

utterances.speaker: KADRI DUGOLI
utterances.text: He brought flour, 4 or 5 litres of oil, one kilogramme of tea, 5, 6 kilogrammes of sugar, pasta, soup, the cigarettes I mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. And to go back a bit in your testimony, I think you mentioned at some point he went to your in-laws because you had too many people at your house. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: KADRI DUGOLI
utterances.text: Yes, because after the 9th of May, after it started -- there were refugees even before the 9th of May, but after this day people began to fled -- to flee their houses. And there were many staying in my house. And when he saw that there were too many staying in my house, he took his family to his in-laws in Bajince. We were about 62 persons in my house, and in total I only had five rooms. There wasn't space enough for all of us, and that's why he took his family.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. I misunderstood. I thought you had said that he went to stay with your in-laws, but you meant his in-laws in Bajince. Correct?

utterances.speaker: KADRI DUGOLI
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Thanks. And you said that was two weeks after this second visit. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: KADRI DUGOLI
utterances.text: Not two weeks after his second visit, but two weeks after he brought his family for the first time in my house, which I said was about the 6th or 8th of May. And then after two weeks, he took his family to his in-laws.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And how far approximately is it to Bajince where his in-laws lived?

utterances.speaker: KADRI DUGOLI
utterances.text: My village and Bajince village are adjoined. From my house to Haradin's in-laws, the distance is approximately 3 to 4 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. And do you remember how they actually made the move over to Mr. Bala's in-laws?

utterances.speaker: KADRI DUGOLI
utterances.text: Haradin's brother took that flour that remained and took it to his in-laws. Some went on foot, some in tractors, some in horse-drawn carts.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Did you go with him?

utterances.speaker: KADRI DUGOLI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thanks very much for your patience with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Black. Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Just one question please, Mr. Dugoli. When Mr. Bala came to your house bringing flour and other goods, other food, did he come alone?

utterances.speaker: KADRI DUGOLI
utterances.text: He came with a friend in a car, Lada make, and he brought the flour because he wasn't able to load or unload that sack of flours -- flour because it weighed 50 kilogrammes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Mr. Dugoli. Thank you very much for your attendance here today.

utterances.speaker: KADRI DUGOLI
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you for your assistance. That completes your questioning. You may now leave and return to your home. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: We will now play musical chairs again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: We will be calling the last witness of the day, Mr. Thaqi.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: While we are waiting in this brief moment I should inform the Chamber that we have potentially two additional witnesses for tomorrow. Apart from that, there will be no further live witnesses called on behalf of Mr. Bala. There is one matter that remains which we are working out with the Prosecution, which is the statement of a gentleman whose name is Howard Tucker and he is submitting a 92 bis statement in regard of Mr. Tucker. At the conclusion of today's proceedings, I would like to, after agreement with the Prosecution, introduce into evidence those medical records that we have been able to obtain with regard to Mr. Bala's medical history.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My greetings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Thaqi, good afternoon. Would you please read aloud the affirmation on the card that's shown to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Please sit down. Mr. Guy-Smith has some questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Thaqi.

utterances.speaker: ALI THAQI
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: How are you today?

utterances.speaker: ALI THAQI
utterances.text: Very well, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excellent. How old are you, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Are you presently working?

utterances.speaker: ALI THAQI
utterances.text: No. I am in the building trade, and I work privately.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Do you know Haradin Bala?

utterances.speaker: ALI THAQI
utterances.text: From the moment I was born.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
