utterances.text: Well, I was going to ask you how long you've known him. Since we know you're 48, I guess you've known him for quite some time.

utterances.speaker: ALI THAQI
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Where do you live, sir?

utterances.speaker: ALI THAQI
utterances.text: In Lapusnik, in my birthplace.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Do you know Haradin Bala's family, by that I mean his father, mother, and brother?

utterances.speaker: ALI THAQI
utterances.text: I know all of them. Haradin's mother is my sister.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: What did Haradin's father do?

utterances.speaker: ALI THAQI
utterances.text: Haradin's father was of a poor health. He had problems with his lungs. He was a singer, a rhapsodic singer. He sang Albanian folk songs.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: When you say he was a singer, a rhapsodic singer, was he known throughout your area or was this just something he did privately?

utterances.speaker: ALI THAQI
utterances.text: How shall I put this? He lived from singing, from this profession. Usually in our country they sing at weddings, and he also participated in different festivals.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Before the war, do you know if Haradin Bala worked?

utterances.speaker: ALI THAQI
utterances.text: Yes. He completed primary school. I don't know if he completed secondary school, electro-technical school, he went for a year or two, and then he worked at a building trade company.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Do you know how long he worked at that building trade company?

utterances.speaker: ALI THAQI
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. Perhaps until the time when workers were dismissed from work.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Could you tell us about what time that was, if you know?

utterances.speaker: ALI THAQI
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know for sure. It must have been I think 1987. I don't know exactly when.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Did Haradin Bala follow in his father's footsteps when it came to song?

utterances.speaker: ALI THAQI
utterances.text: No, he couldn't sing. He tried but he couldn't. He was sick almost all the time. Since he was a child, he started smoking and he left it to me as well as a gift. I learned from him to smoke because, as I said, all my life I have been very close to him. I haven't seen him only for these last two years. I grew up under his umbrella, literally speaking, which he always carried with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, if he didn't sing, did he perchance play any musical instruments?

utterances.speaker: ALI THAQI
utterances.text: Yes, but he didn't play it very much because he was sick. We both gave it a try, myself and him, but we weren't successful.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You mentioned that he was very sick. Could you tell us when the first time is that you can recall him being very sick.

utterances.speaker: ALI THAQI
utterances.text: We are talking about Haradin?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: ALI THAQI
utterances.text: Haradin -- I think he was ill all -- during all the time, but in the 1990s, somewhere in the -- sometime in the 1990s, he became very sick. The first time it happened, he was taken to the neuro-psychiatric hospital. I think his left hand and arm were paralyzed. He stayed there for some time, then he had a heart attack, as the doctor said, and this happened sometime in the 1990s. In 1992 he got ill in my own house. I took him - and I say this in full responsibility because a son of mine was born in 1992 on the 21st of January - and when Haradin got sick in my own house my son was three months old, so it must have been May or June of that year. I took him to his home. He was so ill that I told him I would rather like to see him dead than see him suffer so much from that disease.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I would like to, if I could, show you two photographs and see whether or not you recognise them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And I guess we could put those up on -- yeah, wonderful.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: The first photograph, can you see that photograph?

utterances.speaker: ALI THAQI
utterances.text: It is not very clear, but I ask know it even at night. It's myself, Haradin, and Haradin's younger brother Besim.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And could you tell us when that photograph was taken?

utterances.speaker: ALI THAQI
utterances.text: This was taken during my visit in the hospital. I don't recall the year. It may have been 1990 maybe.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: The -- I notice that the -- Haradin is wearing clothes that are somewhat distinct. Do you know why he's wearing those clothes?

utterances.speaker: ALI THAQI
utterances.text: This was the uniform that patients wear in hospital, as we say pyjamas.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You say you recognise in the photograph Haradin and his younger brother, Besim. Could you tell us in this photograph how old Besim was?

utterances.speaker: ALI THAQI
utterances.text: What can I say, maybe 13, 14 years old.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Could you show him the next picture, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I would like you to take a look at this, it's the second picture, and ask if you recognise the individuals in that photograph.

utterances.speaker: ALI THAQI
utterances.text: Yes, I know them. It's Haradin with his younger brother, Besim, and with his uncle on his father's side, Selman.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Do you know when this picture was taken?

utterances.speaker: ALI THAQI
utterances.text: No, I don't know but since I see that he's wearing pyjamas, probably it's during the time that he was in hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: After Haradin returned from hospital, do you know whether or not he was able to work or not?

utterances.speaker: ALI THAQI
utterances.text: No, he was not able to work. He was travelling in his horse-drawn cart always wearing an umbrella with him because a doctor advised him not to stay in the sun because of his disease. And during all the time I was almost -- during all the time I was with him. And it was very hard for him to walk when he had to, and we used to smoke together.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I want to focus your attention in the year of 1998, and in the month of May. In the month of May, where were you living, sir?

utterances.speaker: ALI THAQI
utterances.text: I have lived in Lapusnik, in my home village, all my life. In February 1998, on the 28th of February, there was the massacre of Likoshan, Qirez, and we, too, were scared of the Serb forces. In Komorane, 3 kilometres away from the place I live, there is a checkpoint. And at that time we started to organise ourselves and stand on guard. We didn't have weapons but just wanted to keep guard and warn the people in case of something happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Did you stay in Lapusnik throughout 1998?

utterances.speaker: ALI THAQI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: When did you leave Lapusnik?

utterances.speaker: ALI THAQI
utterances.text: I removed my family from Lapusnik on the 8th of May, 1998, when the Serb forces left the Komorane checkpoint, there was a battle in Gjurgjice. When they returned from there it was about 4.00 or 5.00 in the afternoon. Our houses are along -- are 100 metres far from the Prishtine-Pej asphalt road. When they were going to Komorane, they shelled incessantly with their PCA -- APCs, correction, and other heavy weapons. I took my family to the house of Haradin Thaqi. In the evening, I took them to Nekovce to some in-laws. Of the next day -- it was the 9th of May. It was Saturday, if I recollect correctly. There was the first battle in Lapusnik. That day, together with a cousin of mine, Bajram Thaqi, having no weapon I went to Vuqak to a sister of mine and waited there until the battle was over. When the battle was over, we returned home in the evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Let me ask you this, sir: Did you ever become a member of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: ALI THAQI
utterances.text: No, I couldn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: ALI THAQI
utterances.text: Because I didn't have a gun.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: In the early part of May, did you have an occasion to see Haradin Bala around Lapusnik?

utterances.speaker: ALI THAQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: When did you see him?

utterances.speaker: ALI THAQI
utterances.text: I have seen him after the 9th of May. He came with an automatic rifle to the room of Musli Haradini. Present were some males aging from 18 to 50. He came with an automatic rifle to join the KLA. I told him that I wanted to go with him, but it was impossible because we couldn't share the same weapon; this cannot be.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: When you saw him sometime after the 9th of May and he was joining the KLA, when is the next time you saw him?

utterances.speaker: ALI THAQI
utterances.text: After May, I saw him sometime in June in Nekovce and in Bajice where his family were -- was staying.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. Please wait there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Mansfield.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: No questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: No questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Topolski. Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm over here, sir. I have a few questions for you. As you stated, you've known Haradin Bala your whole life?

utterances.speaker: ALI THAQI
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You're a close personal friend of his and of his family's?

utterances.speaker: ALI THAQI
utterances.text: Yes, I'm his uncle.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And have you been a co-worker with him?

utterances.speaker: ALI THAQI
utterances.text: We worked together in the building trade.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: When was that that you worked together?

utterances.speaker: ALI THAQI
utterances.text: Before the 1990s.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Were you laid off at the same time when the -- when that company closed?

utterances.speaker: ALI THAQI
utterances.text: I worked in a different enterprise. We didn't work in the same enterprise.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, you stated you never joined the KLA because you didn't have a gun. Right?

utterances.speaker: ALI THAQI
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, you're aware that the KLA issued guns to people, aren't you, including in Lapusnik?

utterances.speaker: ALI THAQI
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware that the KLA issued weapons. Only those who were able to walk, to go on foot, to Albania and get weapons, only those could have weapons. Others couldn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, you know where Gzim Gashi's house is, don't you, in Lapusnik?

utterances.speaker: ALI THAQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You don't know that there was a man in there keeping records on KLA soldiers and one of his jobs was to record who brought their own weapon and who was issued one?

utterances.speaker: ALI THAQI
utterances.text: No, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You -- I'm trying to be clear on your testimony. Was it that you were present when Haradin Bala had an attack or a heart attack of some kind and had to go to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: ALI THAQI
utterances.text: Yes. Haradin was in my house and I was present, yes. This was his second heart attack. After, he was released from hospital because of the first attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Was that in 1990 or in 1993?

utterances.speaker: ALI THAQI
utterances.text: It happened in 1992, possibly in the month of May or June.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And who else was present?

utterances.speaker: ALI THAQI
utterances.text: Myself and my family, my wife, my mother, and others.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Were you aware of whether Haradin Bala had a heart attack in 1993 as well or do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: ALI THAQI
utterances.text: After the first attack, Haradin was frequently ill and he always used pills.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. But that doesn't actually answer the question. Do you know whether he had another attack in 1993?

utterances.speaker: ALI THAQI
utterances.text: Concretely, I don't know. But as of 1992, he was ill on many occasions. I don't remember the year.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And between that period in 1998, you're not aware of him having any other major health complications, heart attacks, anything like that that you're aware of?

utterances.speaker: ALI THAQI
utterances.text: Not specifically, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You said you weren't aware of this record-keeping which took place in Gzim Gashi's oda. Did you go to Gzim Gashi's compound in May, June, July 1998 yourself?

utterances.speaker: ALI THAQI
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And did you go into the compound directly across the street from Gzim Gashi's compound? You didn't, did you?

utterances.speaker: ALI THAQI
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And like everyone else in Lapusnik and from Lapusnik, you regard Haradin Bala and the other accused here as heroes for defending your town. Right?

utterances.speaker: ALI THAQI
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, you've described Haradin Bala as too sick to sing, too sick to play an instrument, just perhaps barely able to hold an umbrella. Is that your testimony? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: ALI THAQI
utterances.text: It's not only my testimony; this is how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Right. But I'm only asking about your testimony. That's the way he was in 1998?

utterances.speaker: ALI THAQI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's the way he was when he was able to walk with a fully-loaded Kalashnikov strung over his shoulder. Right?

utterances.speaker: ALI THAQI
utterances.text: He was sick throughout the time. I didn't see what he was carrying during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: But you testified about him having an automatic rifle. Right? You just finished talking about that?

utterances.speaker: ALI THAQI
utterances.text: Yes. I said that he came to join the KLA. He had an automatic rifle. I wanted to join him, but it wasn't possible for two soldiers to share the same gun; this is what I said earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: He was determined to join the KLA, despite his health condition. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ALI THAQI
utterances.text: With the force left in him, he was determined to go. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And he wasn't even from Lapusnik; he came from Korretice because he was seeking out combat. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ALI THAQI
utterances.text: He wasn't from Lapusnik. Lapusnik and Korretice are 5 kilometres apart. Where Haradin lived, it wasn't possible to combat.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Right. When we knew there was fighting going on in Lapusnik, when it could be heard in his village, he went with his automatic rifle to help. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ALI THAQI
utterances.text: He came, joined, and I don't know where he went and where he fought.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, nothing terrible happened to you for not joining the KLA; it was a volunteer army. Correct?

utterances.speaker: ALI THAQI
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Haradin Bala didn't have to join, he didn't have to come to Lapusnik, the front line. Right?

utterances.speaker: ALI THAQI
utterances.text: If you could repeat the question, please, I didn't understand it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, just like you, Haradin Bala didn't have to come to the front line; he could have stayed in Korretice smoking, holding an umbrella, and not getting anywhere near the combat, correct? But he chose to come and fight.

utterances.speaker: ALI THAQI
utterances.text: None of us wanted a war, but it was imposed on us. There was no way that Haradin could have stayed in Korretice because it's just 5 kilometres away from Lapusnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Were you aware that before he came to Lapusnik he organised some of the guard duty in Korretice and took part in guarding Korretice?

utterances.speaker: ALI THAQI
utterances.text: No, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your testimony is that he would never stay out in the sun? Is that -- you really mean that? He would always avoid the sun at all costs?

utterances.speaker: ALI THAQI
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Well, it's a very small - and I'll grant it - even silly point. The photographs with you, he's outside, no umbrella, squinting into the sun. You're enjoying the sunny day together?

utterances.speaker: ALI THAQI
utterances.text: To me, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, that's right. And it's another example -- I'll suggest to you you're exaggerating all of your testimony about Mr. Bala's health condition because you're trying to help him because he's your friend, he's your relative, and because he fought for the KLA?

utterances.speaker: ALI THAQI
utterances.text: No, that's not right. The doctor recommended to Haradin -- as I said earlier, he was ill. He fell ill in my own house and he was so ill that I said I'd rather see him dead than in this condition.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Nothing further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Nothing further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Thaqi, that completes the questions that are to be asked of you. Thank you for your assistance and you're able now to return to your home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Have a good day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I had mentioned before Mr. Thaqi was called that it was our intention to introduce some exhibits. Initially, I would like to introduce the two photographs, if I could, and have them marked as next in order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: They will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the two photographs will be given Defence Exhibit DB5.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: In addition, we had previously filed, I believe both with the Chamber and supplied a copy with the Prosecution, of those medical records that we have been able to compile with regard to Mr. Bala's health history. And I would like to have those marked collectively as an exhibit, if I could, and I believe we are in agreement to those to go in.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to those exhibits, I would only note to the extent it's of any interest that what is designated as 1.1, which is the medical note from the doctor, which we have a copy of, we do have the original in a tattered form here. I believe the copy is certainly representative, but I wish to make the Court aware of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I take it there's no objection to the photocopies there, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Was it tattered form?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Tattered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It was shown in two pieces.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That is the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Do we have the actual set of medical records?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I believe that you do, but in the event that you don't I have them once again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It's a question of whether the record has a copy. If you could pass them to the --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If I could pass these then and have these exhibited, that way we'll be sure that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Each member of the Chamber has what I believe is a copy of the same --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We need to be sure we have the right thing as the exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes. So this will be received as a bundle of medical records of the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE THELIN
utterances.text: Could I on this have a clarification from you, Mr. Guy-Smith. It seems in the Dutch original there's a reference to a Mr. Lente and it says "slash Bala." I just want to have that clarified.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If we might go into private session for a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in public session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That exhibit is received as DB6, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. With regard to the testimony of the live witnesses, that is the extent of the testimony of the live witnesses we have available for today. Tomorrow we have two witnesses, I believe both of them -- I think one of them has arrived. One of them is in the process of arriving. I understand we start tomorrow morning at 9.00 and we are intending to call them viva voce. And the remaining matter is the matter I raised with the Chamber earlier, which is the statement of Mr. Tucker, which we are in the process of ironing out between the Prosecution and ourselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Then you would like to adjourn now?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, that would be convenient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Topolski, I wasn't meaning to --

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls was on his feet. I don't know if he was bursting to say something or bursting to say good night.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I was just rising.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Topolski, then it's you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know if this will assist. If it doesn't I will say no more now. But I think it was Judge Thelin who asked last week tentatively whether we were in a position to indicate the position regarding the case of Isak Musliu. We are about to reach the end of Mr. Bala's case tomorrow. I am in a position to indicate it now that I understand that the Tribunal would be assisted with regard to its own forward planning to hear what the position is sooner rather than later. Or if it's felt inappropriate to interpose this now, I'm happy to wait until Mr. Guy-Smith is finished tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We'd be happy to hear now, Mr. Topolski.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Your Honours, the position is this: that it is and will be our submission that the Prosecution has failed in this case to prove beyond reasonable doubt any part of this indictment against Isak Musliu. Consequently, he will neither give nor call any live evidence as to the facts in this case. We have agreed a number of witnesses under the 92 bis procedure. There will be a formal filing in due course. I should add this, that there is one expert, Professor Wagenaar, whose statement I think was filed on the 26th of May, dealing with identification procedures, who will be called by me, as it were, on behalf of all three defendants. My learned friends for the Office of the Prosecutor were perfectly entitled to and have sought to stand by the 30-day rule regarding Professor Wagenaar, and consequently, there will be a time delay before one is able to call him. May I indicate, and I hope Mr. Whiting will permit me to do this because it's relevant to your planning, to indicate where I understand we are with regard to that witness. Mr. Whiting tells me that he's not yet in a position to cross-examine him. He has asked for and we have agreed to a conjoint meeting with Professor Wagenaar and representatives of both Prosecution and Defence bars. Mr. Whiting has asked for, and I'm setting this up, for that meeting to take place during the week commencing the week of the 20th of June, in other words not the next week but the week after, and as presently advised by him - Mr. Whiting, that is - he indicated to us that he would not, he thought, be in a position to cross-examine that witness until the week commencing the 27th of June, at the earliest. Now, these are all matters that Mr. Whiting would have to no doubt develop, if called upon to do so. All I wished to indicate, first of all, was what our position was in the case as a whole and what the position is, therefore, that stands between tomorrow and the conclusion of the evidence, and the short answer to that is Professor Wagenaar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And he is on a particular and confined expert --

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Your Honour, there's been a filing and may I respectfully on behalf of the bar invite the Tribunal at a convenient time to read the report of Professor Wagenaar, which happily is not long for an expert. He is not a name unknown to this Tribunal. He has been called in fact by the Prosecution on two previous occasions I think. It's on the issue of identification evidence, which is common to all three defendants here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: And the -- yes, I hear the whisper to my left. The consideration is active between us and learned friends is whether he, as it were, becomes a joint expert before the Tribunal. But I'll say no more about that at the moment because I'm not clear what Mr. Whiting -- yes, Mr. Whiting's position really will be with that regard -- in that regard. So, Your Honour, that, in summary form, is the position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much for that, Mr. Topolski. Thinking -- is there anything that Mr. Whiting would want to add on this theme?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, I would just add that the schedule that's been laid out by Mr. Topolski is essentially accurate. It's possible that things will go more quickly, but I don't expect that to happen. I should also say that just so the record is clear that the expert that's been referred to, Professor Wagenaar, has indeed testified twice at the Tribunal, but on both occasions as a Defence witness, not as a Prosecution witness. I don't frankly expect that he will become a joint witness, but of course anything is possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If I might --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If I might, with the briefest of corrections. He has neither testified only as a Prosecution witness nor only as a Defence witness. As a matter of fact, on one occasion I believe he was agreed to be a witness and was called ultimately as a witness for the Chamber itself by agreement between the Prosecution and Defence. And on one occasion, he was called as a Defence witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, we look forward in due course to hearing the evidence, whether he's been called by anybody else or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, you may wish to call him yourself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We're not in that mood.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: I'm going to try and get you to do it just once before we finish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: If you wanted the Chamber to call witnesses, you might be surprised at the list, Mr. Topolski. Don't provoke, I would advise.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I very briefly, please, and this is not an attempt to take up the next hour and three-quarters with procedural matters. But may I dip my toe into another pool all together, and it's this: The reality is, therefore, that on any view the evidence in this case will finish in this case before the end of next month. On any view. I don't invite discussion on it now, but I know it would help some of us a very great deal to have a discussion at some convenient moment regarding the final stages of the trial that will follow the conclusion of the evidence. As I say, I want to make it clear, I'm not provoking or requesting a discussion of that now necessarily. But may I flag it up as a topic that will certainly need to be discussed for Your Honours to in fact indicate in due course after, I hope, hearing submissions on the subject a timetable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: While your toe is in the water, Mr. Topolski --

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: I hope you're not going to push me in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: No, I was just going to drop a few little blocks of ice and see how you reacted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It would seem highly desirable in the interests in particular of the accused that we reach the end of the trial and a decision as soon as can properly be done so. To that end, it would seem highly desirable that we conclude both the receipt of written submissions and any oral final submissions before the end of the current term, if I can borrow an English expression. That would mean that before the 23rd of July. That -- bearing in mind --

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: This water's getting cold.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Bearing in mind where we now are in June, accepting that there will be the interposition of the evidence of Professor Wagenaar, I venture for the consideration of counsel and perhaps submissions tomorrow, assuming there may be time for that, whether it would be convenient to contemplate then written final cases sometime by about the first full week of July, which concludes on the 8th; and then oral submissions to follow either at the end of the week following or at the beginning of the last week of the term. Now --

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: When Your Honour says that, does the Tribunal -- Chamber have mutual filing in mind?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Um --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That is the practice that has been most usually found convenient and which we have found. Oral submissions enable then a taking up of any disparity and for that reason in particular we would normally think of allowing at least a week between the written filing and the oral.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, perhaps we should address this more fully tomorrow --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, as I indicated, they were merely a few little blocks of ice for people to think of.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I can indicate --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: If they present major problems, we would like to hear about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I try to avoid adjectives whenever possible, but in this case, certainly for me personally, that would produce a major problem. It would require my return from the United States for the purpose of making final submissions to this Tribunal, which of course it would be my pleasure to do if I'm required to do so. I don't know what other problems, logistically, professionally, or personally that presents any of my learned friends. As far as the brief is concerned, may I indicate this without giving away any state secrets. I think it's the intention of the Defence to file a joint brief which will be the most convenient way of receiving it, we think. It will nonetheless be a very considerable document. We are aware that there are page limits to such a document, and we would anticipate that we would reach that limit in any event. So therefore we are talking about the submission of a document of something a little less than 500 pages. In addition to that, final speeches, which certainly for my part and I'm sure for others who defend will not be by way, as it were, of repetition of that brief, but by way of amplification of submission of the contents of the final brief. Major undertaking, thereto, in the consideration and preparation of that, I can tell the Tribunal -- Chamber that there are a team of volunteers and conscripts actively engaged on this, this process -- of preparation of the final brief I mean. I wouldn't want the Chamber to think that we waited for the conclusion of the evidence to start the work; far from it. The work has been ongoing for some time and I have no doubt Mr. Whiting would say the same on behalf of the team he leads. But, Your Honour, as I say, perhaps we could develop this a little more tomorrow. I think there will be serious concerns as to whether the timetable -- which I very much hope is not written in stone. It doesn't sound like it is. Your Honour didn't describe it that way and I see you're --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It's not. Ice has a habit of melting under any sort of heat.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: I hope I have turned the temperature up very slightly. Can I say also that I would not want anyone who sits behind me to think that the object of this exercise to prolong the agony, and I use the term mutually, for any of them any longer than is necessary, and I put it no higher nor lower for us all to discharge our duties to our lay clients and present their cases in the best and most tenable light possible. And that is not a task as to what is required here that can be taken quickly or lightly. Nonetheless, we will not drag our heels over it. Your Honour, with those thoughts very much off the top of my head in response to Your Honour in mind and unless anyone wants to add anything now, that's certainly all I wish to say on the subject this evening. Thank you for the opportunity of being heard on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I fancy it may be something for counsel to reflect on and be ready tomorrow with views. You keep hiding behind these new screens, Mr. Whiting. Is there anything you feel you need to put into play at this moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: No, I understand this is something we will take up tomorrow. Just so there's no suspense, I anticipate that we'll say that it will be extraordinarily difficult to meet that deadline. There may be even a brief rebuttal case, though I wouldn't expect that that would take more than a day or two. That would be completed the week of the 27th --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Along with the evidence and cross-examination of the professor?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I would expect, yes, Your Honour, assuming the professor testifies on Monday, I assume that would be completed by the end of the week. That leaves only one week to devote full attention to the final brief which --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, I venture the thought that time is now running largely with respect to that rather than waiting until the end of the professor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: No, that's certainly true, though up until today and up until tomorrow we've been busy with the Defence case and we will continue to be busy preparing for the expert. We have been -- we have been working -- the team we have is essentially what you have before you here in the courtroom. And we haven't waited to start. We have been underway, but nonetheless there's always a lot to pull together at the end, a lot to just simply write. So -- I'm just anticipating what our position will be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well. I think we have aired the issue enough today to start thoughts running. And with that in mind, we would look forward tomorrow to the further evidence and then to submissions on this issue which is, as Mr. Topolski has indicated, a serious one which requires the balancing of the desirability of reaching finality in this trial at the earliest proper opportunity, with the need of ensuring that counsel have time to put their respective cases forward in a proper form so that justice is best aided. With that in mind, we will adjourn now until tomorrow at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 8th day of June, 2005, at 9.00 a.m. 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 5.31 p.m.,
